newsitem.title: LEBANON: Vote consolidates Hariri's power, despite flaws.
newsitem.headline: Vote consolidates Hariri's power, despite flaws.

text.p: Even if voting has been marred by alleged bribery and fraud, Lebanon's parliamentary elections have gone a long way towards consolidating Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri's power as the country's dominant politician.

The new parliament emerging from the five-stage election will feature a strong bloc of Hariri supporters and a new set of political alliances, and it is likely to give Hariri greater freedom of action than the outgoing chamber, Beirut political analysts said.
In particular, it should ease restraints on the accumulation of foreign debt to finance reconstruction projects which Hariri wants to push ahead after being blocked by the old parliament, they said.

Hariri, a construction tycoon who made his money in Saudi Arabia, has often been criticised for lack of political skills since assuming public office for the first time in October 1992 as prime minister.
His success in Sunday's third-round vote in Beirut should make the critics think again.

It gave him the solid electoral base he sought, as he won the highest number of votes in the capital, and made him a dominant figure in parliament as he and his supporters won 14 of the 19 Beirut seats in the 128-member house.
His supporters won seven seats in earlier voting and should pick up two or three more in the final two rounds.
In a country that lacks national political parties, that means Hariri will head the biggest or second biggest bloc in parliament by the time the elections end on September 15.
"The new parliament will be different from the old. Hariri will have a big say in it," said a Beirut political analyst who asked not to be identified.
Businessmen say that is good news for the stability of the Lebanese pound, which is in effect pegged to Hariri's political fortunes, and for the future of the reconstruction drive.

The last parliament shelved many of Hariri's projects, reluctant to let the government accumulate too much debt. Hariri twice threatened to resign and once stepped down briefly, accusing the Shi'ite Moslem speaker Nabih Berri of sabotage.
But Hariri now has a solid electoral alliance with Berri, who headed the biggest bloc in the old parliament and is likely to have another big bloc in the new parliament.

"So embarking into new debt won't be as hard as it was in the old parliament, particularly as Berri is now very much in favour of infrastructure projects and is getting a bigger and bigger share in them," an analyst said.
One indication of the solid base of the new Hariri-Berri alliance was the award of a $225 million contract for a new motorway from the southern city of Sidon to Naqoura near the Israeli border.
The contract was quietly awarded, without a public tender, to Hariri's brother Shafiq and Berri's wife Randa with the Syrian contractor Kassyoun, the analyst said.

"I don't think Berri is now going to be reluctant to allow parliament to permit new infrastructure projects and borrowing," the analyst said. "Profit margins in Lebanese infrastructure projects are above 40 percent."
Despite emerging stronger in parliament, Hariri has failed to achieve all his election aims and will still face opposition after having campaigned for a "unified" parliament.
His two main rivals in Beirut, ex-premier Selim Hoss and Christian radical Najah Wakim both won seats, preventing Hariri from claiming the uncontested leadership of the capital.
Both rivals expressed indignation at "scandalous" electoral abuses. Wakim vowed to sue Hariri, his supporters and Interior Minister Michel al-Murr who organised the polls.

Newspapers also noted that 70 percent of Beirut voters stayed away in an indication of disillusionment with Lebanese democracy and indicated that a big question mark would hang over the credibility of the new parliament.

"Elections in Lebanon are gradually becoming an unprecedented farce and a joke," the anti-government newspaper Ad-Diyar said. "From Mount Lebanon to the north and then Beirut, the polls are becoming less credible and more of a mockery and no one knows how they will end in the south and the Bekaa valley."
